instance_recommendations.rationale: AMD EPYC-based equivalent of c5.2xlarge with identical vCPU/memory specs at ~10% lower cost. Best price-performance ratio for compute-bound Celery workloads. Drop-in replacement with no architectural changes needed.

Newer-generation AMD instance with improved per-core performance over c5a at nearly the same price point. Offers a good balance of modern hardware benefits and cost savings. Slightly better single-threaded performance than c5a.
Current baseline instance type. Well-proven for this workload. No migration risk but offers no cost savings.

Same price as c5.2xlarge but built on 3rd-gen Intel Xeon (Ice Lake) with ~15% better compute performance. Effectively offers more throughput per dollar at the same cost, which could reduce the number of instances needed at peak.

rationale.scaling_policy: The step thresholds are aligned to the observed queue depth distribution. With p50=0 and 78% zero-depth time, the first step (0–1) aggressively scales down by -3 to quickly shed idle capacity during the dominant quiet periods. The 1–50 step (+5) handles the common small bursts that represent typical work arrival. The 50–200 step (+10) addresses moderate load. A new 200–800 step (+20) bridges the gap around the p95 value of ~841 messages, ensuring adequate ramp-up before the queue grows further. The 800–5000 step (+35) provides strong scaling through the transition zone between p95 and p99 (31,323). The final unbounded step at 5000+ (+55) enables rapid scale-out toward the max capacity of 120 to handle the extreme bursts observed up to 54,617 messages. The previous policy had a maximum adjustment of +15 which was insufficient given that the ASG historically hit its max_desired of 120, indicating the policy struggled to keep up with burst arrivals.
rationale.strategy_impact: The balanced strategy influenced the design by: (1) Setting cooldown at 300 seconds — the minimum required by instance_drain_seconds — which prevents thrashing while still allowing responsive scaling every 5 minutes. This avoids the overly aggressive approach of a performance strategy while being faster than a cost-focused strategy might dictate. (2) Using moderate scale-down of -3 rather than -1 (too slow/costly) or -5+ (too aggressive/risky). (3) Adding two additional high-threshold steps (800–5000 and 5000+) compared to the original policy to provide more granular and proportionate responses to the wide range of observed queue depths (0 to 54,617). (4) Recommending c5a.2xlarge as the top choice — it provides the best absolute cost savings without sacrificing any meaningful performance, representing the optimal price-performance trade-off.
rationale.risk_notes: 1. The queue is at zero 78.17% of the time but the policy cannot scale to zero (min_size=1), which is appropriate since zero-depth is below the 80% safety threshold. 2. The observed max_desired reached 120 (the current max_size ceiling), meaning during peak bursts the ASG was capacity-constrained. Consider monitoring whether 120 remains sufficient; if queue depth persists at high levels even at max capacity, max_size may need to increase. 3. The 300-second cooldown means during extreme burst scenarios (queue jumping from 0 to 50,000+), it takes multiple scaling cycles (~15-20 minutes) to reach full capacity. This is an acceptable trade-off for balanced strategy but will result in temporary queue buildup during sudden spikes. 4. Switching to c5a.2xlarge (AMD) should be validated with application testing to ensure no AMD-specific compatibility issues, though for Python/Celery workloads this is extremely unlikely. 5. The scale-down adjustment of -3 combined with 300s cooldown means draining from 120 to 1 instance takes approximately 200 minutes (~3.3 hours) in the absence of new work, which balances cost savings against the risk of scaling down too quickly before a subsequent burst.
